description: Autumn does not invent the colors. It removes the green that was hiding them. Behind the show sits a survival plan for getting through winter.

hero.hook: Autumn leaves are not putting on makeup. They are taking off the green.

blocks.text: Every autumn, forests turn from green to gold, copper, and purple. This is not a matter of taste. It is a strategy: the tree takes back what it can before dropping its leaves for winter.
The warm colors do not appear out of nowhere. Often they were already there, hidden under the green. To understand autumn is to understand a huge biochemical cleanup.

From spring to late summer, leaves are packed with **chlorophyll**, the pigment that powers photosynthesis. Light breaks it down, but the tree keeps replacing it. As long as it dominates, the leaf stays green.

blocks.caption: In autumn, chlorophyll fades and reveals the colors of the leaves

blocks.text: But the leaf also holds **carotenoids**, the yellow and orange pigments (the same ones as in a carrot). In summer they are present, just invisible under the green. In autumn, chlorophyll production stops. The green fades, and the yellow and orange come out.
“Chlorophyll” comes from the Greek *chloros* (green) and *phyllon* (leaf). “Carotenoid” shares its root with the carrot, where the pigment was first identified.

Cold is not the main thing that starts autumn. The length of the nights is. Trees measure it with light sensors called [[phytochromes]]. As the nights stretch out, a hormonal signal travels to every leaf.

At the base of the leaf stalk, a [[separation zone (abscission)]] forms, a kind of plug. Less sap comes up, and the sugars struggle to go back down. Cut off, the leaf breaks down its chlorophyll faster. The more stable yellows hold for a few weeks, then the leaf falls.

sections.title: The real trigger: nights that grow longer

blocks.text: The yellow was already there. Red and purple, on the other hand, are often **made** at the end of the season. These are the [[Anthocyanins]], produced when sugars stay trapped in the leaf.

Why spend energy just before throwing the leaf away? Probably to **protect** it during the recycling work. The tree reclaims **nitrogen** and other valuable nutrients. Without chlorophyll, sunlight can damage the tissue that is still working. Anthocyanins act like a sunscreen for the length of the big move down to the roots.

sections.title: Where the bright reds come from

blocks.text: The finest reds usually come from sunny days followed by cool nights without frost. Plenty of sugar, and it gets turned into anthocyanins. A gray, rainy autumn gives duller shades. An early frost kills the leaves before the show.

At the end, little is left but the [[tannins]], the brown substances of the forest floor. Some studies also suspect that bright colors are a warning to [[aphids]]: this tree is healthy, its defenses are strong, better go elsewhere.
Autumn reveals the yellows that were already there once the chlorophyll is gone, and sometimes makes red to protect the recycling of nutrients before the leaves fall.
